analysis.one_liner: Requires a seven-day waiting period and a police check before someone buys a handgun.
analysis.headline: The first Brady bill, introduced in late 1991, never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until Congress ended, though the idea became law in 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for a licensed gun dealer to hand over a handgun until at least seven days had passed and the buyer's local chief law enforcement officer — usually the police chief or sheriff — had been notified and had not reported that the buyer is legally barred from owning a gun. Buyers would sign a sworn statement listing the federal disqualifications, like a felony conviction or being a fugitive. The waiting period could be skipped if the buyer already has a verified permit, lives in a state with its own waiting period or check, or needs a gun because of a specific threat to their life.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who might be shot by someone who would have failed a background check — in practice, the general public. Lawful buyers would get a built-in cooling-off period, and people facing an immediate threat could bypass the wait. Local police would gain a window to flag prohibited buyers before a sale goes through.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The general public and crime victims

how_it_helps.text: Requires licensed dealers to wait at least seven days after a buyer submits a sworn statement before transferring a handgun, during which local law enforcement can flag a prohibited purchase [S2][S3].

Makes buyers attest under oath that they are not disqualified — for example, no felony conviction or pending indictment, not a fugitive, not unlawfully using controlled substances, not involuntarily committed [S2][S3].

Allows the waiting period to be bypassed when the buyer has a state permit issued within five years under a verified licensing law, or presents a statement from law enforcement that they need a handgun because of a threat to their life or a household member's [S2][S3].

Protects buyer privacy: the dealer must send the buyer's statement to the local chief law enforcement officer, who must destroy it within 30 days unless the transaction would violate the law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Licensed handgun dealers, importers, and manufacturers would handle the paperwork, verify identification, and delay every non-exempt sale by at least a week. Gun buyers would wait. Local police departments would process the notifications with no added funding.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun dealers, buyers, and local police

drawbacks.text: A one-week delay falls on every lawful buyer, and the burden of running the checks falls on already busy local police chiefs and sheriffs, with no new funding attached [S2][S3].
The bill covers handguns only — no waiting period or check for rifles or shotguns — so the mechanisms it targets can be evaded by switching weapon types [S3].
Compliance rests heavily on the buyer's self-reported statement, and the penalty for knowingly violating it is small: a fine of up to $1,000, up to one year in prison, or both [S3].
A good-faith objection from gun-rights advocates is that a waiting period delays honest purchases while someone determined to obtain a gun illegally simply avoids licensed dealers altogether.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a simple, low-cost screening window that lets police catch prohibited buyers — people with felony records, outstanding warrants, or drug addictions — before a handgun changes hands. The costs are real but modest: a week's wait for lawful buyers, paperwork for dealers, and unfunded work for local police. The main design weaknesses are that it covers only handguns and leans on a buyer's self-attestation rather than an instant records check.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, and it sat there until the 102nd Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on November 26, 1991, and it was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice, which is where the record ends [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors and never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S4][S5].
This was the first version of what became the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, named for James Brady; a successor version passed and was signed into law later in 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed handgun dealers and opponents of waiting periods were better off, since no waiting period took effect during this Congress. The public lost the safety measure for another two years, though the idea survived and became law the following year.

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.role: Sponsor; member of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over firearms law
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction, sent it to the crime subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Led public opposition to waiting-period legislation during this era, opposing the Brady bill's approach.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The lone sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan alignment either way.

industries.industry: Licensed firearms dealers, importers, and manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have added a mandatory seven-day delay and paperwork to every non-exempt handgun sale, slowing transactions and shifting compliance work onto dealers. Its failure left those transaction practices untouched. Dealers' interest in blocking it ran against the public's interest in screening sales.

industries.industry: Local law enforcement agencies (police chiefs and sheriffs)
industries.note: The bill would have required them to receive buyer statements, run disqualifying-record checks, and destroy records within 30 days — new unfunded duties, but ones aimed at the same public-safety outcome as the bill itself.
